title: Ἑρμῆς καὶ Τειρεσίας
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 110 (= Perry 89). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἑρμῆς βουλόμενος τὴν Τειρεσίου μαντικὴν πειρᾶσαι εἰ ἀληθής ἐστι, κλέψας αὐτοῦ τοὺς βόας ἐξ ἀγροῦ, ἧκε πρὸς αὐτὸν εἰς ἄστυ, ὁμοιωθεὶς ἀνθρώπῳ, καὶ ἐπεξενώθη παρ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr: Hermēs boulomenos tēn Teiresiou mantikēn peirasai ei alēthēs esti, klepsas autou tous boas ex agrou, hēke pros auton eis asty, homoiōtheis anthrōpōi, kai epexenōthē par’ autōi.
sentences.l: Hermes, wishing to test the prophetic art of Teiresias, whether it is true, having stolen his oxen out of the field, came to him into the town, made like a man, and was received as a guest in his house.
sentences.i: Hermes, wishing to try whether the prophetic art of Teiresias was genuine, stole his oxen out of the fields, came to him in the town in the likeness of a man, and was taken into his house as a guest.
sentences.n: Teiresias is the blind Theban seer, the most famous of Greek prophets, and his art is the reading of birds — which is what the fable turns on. πειρᾶσαι εἰ … ἐστι is an indirect question keeping the present indicative of the direct one. ἐπεξενώθη is passive: he was made a ξένος, a guest-friend, in the house — the binding relation of host and guest, which makes the theft worse than a theft.

sentences.t: Παραγγελθείσης δὲ τῷ Τειρεσίᾳ τῆς τοῦ ζεύγους ἀπωλείας, παραλαβὼν τὸν Ἑρμῆν, ἧκεν εἰς τὸ προαστεῖον, οἰωνόν τινα περὶ τῆς κλοπῆς σκεψόμενος, καὶ τούτῳ παρῄνει λέγειν ὅ τι ἂν θεάσηται ὄρνεον.
sentences.tr: Parangeltheisēs de tōi Teiresiāi tēs tou zeugous apōleias, paralabōn ton Hermēn, hēken eis to proasteion, oiōnon tina peri tēs klopēs skepsomenos, kai toutōi parēinei legein ho ti an theasētai orneon.
sentences.l: And the loss of the yoke of oxen having been reported to Teiresias, taking Hermes along, he came to the outskirts of the town, meaning to look for some omen concerning the theft, and he urged him to tell whatever bird he might see.
sentences.i: When the loss of his yoke of oxen was reported to Teiresias, he took Hermes with him and went out to the edge of the town to look for an omen about the theft, telling him to report whatever bird he saw.
sentences.n: Παραγγελθείσης … τῆς ἀπωλείας is another genitive absolute. σκεψόμενος is the future participle of purpose, 'in order to look for'. οἰωνός is at once the bird and the sign it carries; the seer's whole business is to read the one out of the other. ὅ τι ἂν θεάσηται is the indefinite relative with ἄν and the subjunctive — 'whatever he might see'.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ Ἑρμῆς τὸ μὲν πρῶτον θεασάμενος ἀετὸν ἐξ ἀριστερῶν ἐπὶ δεξιὰ παριπτάμενον, ἀπήγγειλεν αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr: Kai ho Hermēs to men prōton theasamenos aeton ex aristerōn epi dexia pariptamenon, apēngeilen autōi.
sentences.l: And Hermes, first catching sight of an eagle flying past from the left toward the right, reported it to him.
sentences.n: In Greek augury the quarter decides the sign: the right is the favourable side, and a bird crossing to it from the left brings good. The eagle is Zeus' own bird. Teiresias sets the omen aside all the same.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ εἰπόντος μὴ πρὸς αὐτοὺς τοῦτον εἶναι, ἐκ δευτέρου ἰδὼν κορώνην ἐπί τινος δένδρου καθημένην, καὶ ποτὲ μὲν ἄνω βλέπουσαν, ποτὲ δὲ εἰς γῆν κύπτουσαν, ἐδήλωσεν αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr: Tou de eipontos mē pros autous touton einai, ek deuterou idōn korōnēn epi tinos dendrou kathēmenēn, kai pote men anō blepousan, pote de eis gēn kyptousan, edēlōsen autōi.
sentences.l: And he having said that this one was not for them, a second time, seeing a crow settled upon a tree, and now looking upward, now stooping toward the earth, he made it plain to him.
sentences.i: When Teiresias said that this sign was not for them, Hermes looked a second time, saw a crow perched on a tree, now looking up, now stooping toward the ground, and told him of it.
sentences.n: The infinitive of indirect statement normally keeps the οὐ of the direct words; the μή here is the looser usage of later Greek, which spreads μή to infinitives of every kind. ἐκ δευτέρου is 'for the second time'. The crow's alternation between sky and earth is the whole of the sign, and Teiresias reads it out in the next line.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ὑποτυχὼν ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ αὕτη γε ἡ κορώνη διόμνυται τόν τε Οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν Γῆν ὅτι, ἂν σὺ θέλῃς, τοὺς ἐμαυτοῦ βόας ἀπολήψομαι. »
sentences.tr: Ho de hypotychōn ephē· « All’ hautē ge hē korōnē diomnytai ton te Ouranon kai tēn Gēn hoti, an sy thelēis, tous emautou boas apolēpsomai. »
sentences.l: And he, taking-up-the-word, said: « Why, this crow at least swears by both Heaven and Earth that, if you are willing, I shall get my own oxen back. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχών is the collection's regular word for taking up the word in reply; it is not a physical seizing. διόμνυμαι takes the accusative of the powers sworn by — in Greek one swears the gods rather than by them, and the crow's glances up and down are read as an oath sworn by Heaven above and Earth below. The point of the answer is the ἂν σὺ θέλῃς: the seer names his guest as the thief without naming him.

sentences.t: Τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ χρήσαιτο ἄν τις πρὸς ἄνδρα κλέπτην.
sentences.tr: Toutōi tōi logōi chrēsaito an tis pros andra kleptēn.
sentences.l: This story someone might use against a thieving man.
sentences.i: One might use this story against a thief.
sentences.n: χρήσαιτο ἄν τις is the potential optative, 'one might use'; χράομαι takes the dative of the thing used, τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ.
